title: AI Systems and Use Cases
summary: This intermediate-level module enables learners to distinguish an AI capability from a use case, define an AI system boundary, and select evaluation criteria based on operational context. After completing it, learners can create a structured use-case record that connects system outputs to people, decisions, consequences, and risk controls.
objectives: Distinguish an AI capability, an AI system, and a use case.
Describe an AI system boundary that includes data, computational components, interfaces, people, and downstream processes.
Document a use case in terms of its objective, participants, operating environment, resulting actions, and possible consequences.
Choose evaluation criteria that address both output performance and effects in the surrounding workflow.
Explain why the same capability can require different controls in different use cases.

sections.title: Currency update
paragraphs: The prior cited source record, content/modules/ai-foundations/ai-systems-and-use-cases.json, had an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. It therefore could not provide a resolvable, independently reviewable source for this module.

That source record has been replaced with the National Institute of Standards and Technology publication Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) and its official publication page. The change affects the sourcing of the module's definitions, system-boundary guidance, and risk-based evaluation guidance.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes basic familiarity with data, models, inputs, outputs, and evaluation metrics, but it does not require expertise in model development or a dependency on another catalogue module.
The focus is not a particular provider or product. The goal is to analyze an AI-enabled workflow in a form that supports design review, evaluation, deployment decisions, and risk management.

sections.title: Capability, system, and use case
paragraphs: A capability describes a type of function, such as producing a prediction, recommendation, or decision-related output. A capability alone does not identify who will use the output, the conditions of use, or what will happen next.

An AI system includes more than a computational model. For practical analysis, the system boundary can include input data, computational components, interfaces, human participants, operating procedures, downstream actions, monitoring, and feedback. The boundary should be broad enough to include the parts that can change the real-world result.

A use case connects a capability to a specific objective and operating context. A useful use-case record identifies the objective, intended users, people affected by the system, environment, inputs, output, resulting action, degree of human involvement, possible consequences, and monitoring needs.

Keeping these concepts separate prevents a common reasoning error. Evidence that a capability works under one set of conditions does not by itself establish that every system using that capability is suitable for every use case.

sections.title: Trace the complete workflow
paragraphs: Begin with the objective rather than the model. State the result the organization is trying to achieve and identify the people who use the system or may be affected by it.

Next, trace the path from input to output and from output to action. Record where data originates, how the output is presented, who interprets it, whether a person can question or override it, and which action follows. Also record feedback that may influence later operation.

Then identify foreseeable failure paths. An output may be inaccurate, used outside its intended context, misunderstood by a user, delivered too late, or connected to an inappropriate downstream action. A narrow evaluation of the output can miss these workflow failures.
The resulting system boundary should be explicit. If a person, interface, procedure, or downstream process can materially affect the outcome, excluding it from the analysis requires justification.
sections.callout: Treat the model output as one event in a workflow, not as the final real-world outcome.

sections.title: Match evaluation to context
paragraphs: Evaluation criteria should follow from the documented use case. Output performance matters, but an intermediate system review also considers validity and reliability, safety, security and resilience, accountability and transparency, explainability and interpretability, privacy, and the management of harmful bias. The relative importance of these characteristics depends on the context and consequences of use.

For each criterion, specify what evidence is needed, the conditions under which it will be collected, and what result would be acceptable. Also identify who has authority to approve use, restrict use, pause operation, or respond to a failure.

The same capability can require different controls in different use cases. A low-consequence advisory workflow and a workflow that strongly influences access to an important service can differ in required evidence, human review, monitoring, and response procedures even when their underlying capability is similar.
A sound review therefore asks two separate questions: whether the output performs adequately under relevant conditions, and whether the complete system is appropriate for the documented use case.

sections.title: Build a reviewable use-case record
paragraphs: A reviewable use-case record should state the objective, capability, intended users, affected people, operating environment, input sources, output, downstream action, human role, system boundary, evaluation criteria, foreseeable failures, monitoring approach, and response authority.

Each entry should be specific enough for another reviewer to understand what is inside the assessment and what is outside it. If the objective, environment, users, downstream action, or consequences change, revisit the evaluation instead of assuming that previous evidence still applies.

After completing this module, a learner can move from a general statement that a system has a capability to a structured account of where it will operate, how its output will influence action, what evidence is required, and which controls should surround its use.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a capability from a use case?
choices: A capability describes a type of function, while a use case connects that function to an objective, participants, environment, actions, and consequences.
A capability includes every human and organizational process, while a use case describes only the computational model.
A capability and a use case are interchangeable whenever they produce the same output.
A use case is only the name assigned to an evaluation metric.
questions.explanation: The module defines a capability as a type of function and a use case as that function situated within a specific objective and operating context.

questions.prompt: Which system boundary is most appropriate for analyzing real-world outcomes?
choices: Only the computational model
Only the input data and computational model
The data, computational components, interfaces, people, procedures, downstream actions, monitoring, and feedback that can affect the outcome
Only the final action taken after an output is produced
questions.explanation: The module states that the boundary should include the components and participants that can materially change the real-world result.

questions.prompt: Why can the same capability require different controls in two use cases?
choices: Because every use case must use a different computational model
Because objectives, operating conditions, affected people, downstream actions, and consequences can differ
Because output performance is irrelevant outside model development
Because controls are determined only by the name of the capability
questions.explanation: The module explains that context and consequences determine the evidence, human review, monitoring, and response procedures a use case needs.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation approach is most complete according to the module?
choices: Measure output performance and ignore how the output is used.
Review the user interface without testing outputs.
Evaluate output performance under relevant conditions and assess whether the complete workflow is appropriate for the use case.
Approve the capability once and apply that approval to every future context.
questions.explanation: The module requires both evaluation of the output and assessment of the complete system, including its workflow, context, consequences, and controls.

questions.prompt: What did this currency update change?
choices: It replaced an unverified local source record with resolvable official sources and updated the grounding for definitions, system boundaries, and risk-based evaluation.
It introduced a named commercial product and required configuration.
It removed the need to analyze people and downstream actions.
It changed the module from intermediate to advanced.
questions.explanation: The currency-update section identifies the unverified prior source record, the official replacement sources, and the instructional material affected by that correction.
